1:
That Paul calls himself a servant and not an apostle is noticed first. Chrysostom says he writes to these as to men of equal honour and does not set down his rank of teacher, though servant is itself a great rank, the sum of all good things; where he had many things to order, as with the Corinthians, he assumed his apostleship, but here he gives them no injunctions but such as they could perceive of themselves. Clarke observes the same omission in this letter and in those to the Thessalonians and Philemon, and accounts for it by saying that in none of those places was his apostolical authority in question. Wesley makes it familiarity, under a common title joining his son Timothy with himself. Gill and Henry take the joining of Timothy for humility, an older man honouring a younger, and both insist that Timothy had no hand in composing the letter and was at most the amanuensis, though Clarke notes the subscription gives that office to Epaphroditus.

Barnes prefaces the chapter with the town's history. Philippi took its name from the father of Alexander, who refounded an older Thasian settlement called Crenides from the springs out of the mountains, the Thasians having been drawn there by the gold and silver mines, on the great road from Asia to Europe. There the fate of the Roman empire was decided, when Cassius, supposing all lost, killed himself and Brutus wept over him as the last of the Romans, then lost the second battle and fell on his attendant's sword. But Barnes will not let the battle be the reason for remembering the town: Philippi was the first place in Europe where the gospel was preached, and that invests it with more importance than the battle does. He adds that two American missionaries visited the ruins in May 1834, saw what may have been the market-place where Paul and Silas were beaten, and found the road from Neapolis still paved. Clarke leans on a modern critic for the letter's consistency with the history in Acts, and says it is written in a pleasing and easy style bearing evidence of the contented mind the apostle was then in; Henry adds that this is the only one of Paul's epistles in which no censure is implied or expressed.

The greeting to bishops and deacons draws five opinions. Henry says the apostle acknowledges but two orders, and that whoever considers how the same titles, qualifications and acts of office are ascribed to bishops and presbyters alike will find it hard to make them distinct in scripture times. Clarke is blunter: much paper has been wasted asking how one city could have several bishops, and the answer that Philippi was a metropolitan see is the extravagance of trifling; no such officer is meant as we now term bishop. Robertson agrees that in the second century the word came to mean one superior to elders but not so in the New Testament, and explains the plural by there being usually one church in a city with several pastors. Wesley says the names were used promiscuously in the first ages, and that the apostolic epistles were sent more directly to the churches than to their pastors. Calvin allows that order cannot be maintained among ministers without one presiding, but only in particular bodies, not whole provinces and much less the whole world; the later restriction of the name arose from a human custom resting on no Scripture authority, and from that corruption one man under a new appellation usurped dominion over colleagues called to the same office. Ellicott traces the words to their origins, presbyter a Jewish title of dignity from the synagogue and bishop a title of official duty from secular Greek, and grants they are used indifferently; but he holds this in no way weakens the development of the Episcopate early in the second century.
3:
The note struck at the outset is joy. Wesley observes that after Ephesians, where love reigns, follows this one where there is perpetual mention of joy, and sums the letter in four words: I rejoice, rejoice ye. Robertson calls joy the keynote and points out that Paul is a happy prisoner, as at Philippi itself when he and Silas sang praises at midnight. Henry presses it harder: at Philippi the apostle was scourged and put in the stocks and saw little fruit of his labour, yet he remembers the place with joy, counting his sufferings for Christ his credit and his crown, so far from being ashamed that the very mention of the town was grateful to him. Barnes notes the emphasis of the words, that with so many other churches to remember he never forgot this one, and that all is repeated industriously, to show he loved them equally and to draw the same love from them. Calvin distinguishes the halves, remembrance looking to the past and prayer to the future, so that we rejoice in blessings received in such a way as to remember to ask for what we still need. Clarke reports another rendering, for all your kind remembrance, referring it to their supplying his wants.

What the fellowship in the gospel means is disputed, and Barnes sets out the field: some take it of sharing in the blessings of the gospel, some of constancy in the faith, some of liberality in contributing to its support; he decides for the last, because it accords with the scope of a letter written largely to acknowledge their gifts, and because the word properly denotes what is held in common and passes into the sense of contribution. He adds that from the first day until now rules out the sense of merely acceding to the gospel, the fellowship being something constant. Gill agrees and takes it of their communication to its support, instancing Lydia and the jailer and the present sent by Epaphroditus, though he allows participation as well. Henry argues the other way, that comparing Paul's thanksgivings for other churches it seems rather to be taken generally, of the fellowship they had in faith and hope and holy love.

The sixth verse is where the chapter first touches doctrine. Barnes rests the whole on the fact that God began the work: had it depended on man there could be no sure evidence that any would reach heaven, since nothing a man does today guarantees what he will do tomorrow. His reasons are that God had a design in beginning, that no reason can be given why he should abandon it, and that God abandons nothing he undertakes, there being no unfinished worlds or systems and no half-made and forsaken works of his hands. Calvin puts it as a syllogism, that God does not forsake the work his own hands began, that we are the work of his hands by the calling through which we are adopted, and therefore he will complete what he began; but he then asks how one man can be certain of another's salvation, and answers that the assurance of faith remains inwardly shut up, so that of our neighbours we judge only from the outward efficacy of the Spirit, which is enough to stir up good hope and keep us from an unkind judgment. Robertson and Ellicott both add the qualification, Robertson that God will consummate it but not without their partnership, Ellicott that grace is the beginning and the end while man's co-operation lies in the process linking them. Wesley reads the work as sanctification following justification, carried on till it issue in glory. Calvin ends by carrying the completion past death to the resurrection, since those freed from the body have not reached what they aspire to, and the day has not yet shone that will discover the treasures lying hid in hope.
7:
The clause about the heart is ambiguous and they divide over it. Barnes notes that the Greek will bear either I have you in my heart or ye have me in yours, and takes the former as more obvious; Ellicott agrees and says that both the order and the context are decisive. Robertson refuses to choose: there is no way of deciding except that love begets love, and the pastor who holds his people in his heart will find them holding him in theirs. Henry gives both, and draws from the second that the truest mark of respect towards ministers is abiding by the doctrine they preach. Clarke, following an earlier annotator, refers it to what the Philippians had done, setting their hearts on him in his bonds, sending Epaphroditus to minister to him and contributing of their own substance once and again.

On being partakers of grace the readings part again. Barnes takes it that having made common cause with him in trouble they would share the divine favour attending his labours. Ellicott prefers the margin, partakers with me of the grace, identifying it with the grace given him to preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ, and pointing forward to the later verse where suffering itself is given as a grace. Robertson borrows another's summary, that grace prompted them to alleviate his imprisonment, co-operate in defending the gospel and suffer for its sake. Calvin builds the most on it. In the view of the world it is ludicrous to reckon a prison a benefit from God, yet it is no common honour that God confers when we suffer persecution for his truth, so the fellowship of the cross must be embraced as a special favour; and since God has entrusted us with the defence of his gospel, those called to confess should remember that Christ has chosen them as advocates to plead his cause. He then asks whether the confirmation of the gospel can depend on the steadfastness of men, and answers that the truth of God is too firm to need support from any other quarter, since though all men were liars God remains true, but that weak consciences are confirmed by such helps, the martyrs being so many seals by which the gospel is sealed in our hearts. He quotes the saying that the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the Church, and adds that he imitated it in a Latin poem of his own.

The oath that follows is examined rather than passed over. Chrysostom says he calls God to witness not as though doubted but out of great affection, and adds that had he been flattering them he would not have called God to witness, since that cannot be done without peril. Ellicott lists the other places where the same adjuration occurs and says they show how the apostle understood the command to swear not at all. Gill treats it as an appeal to the searcher of hearts; Robertson notes the same oath in Romans. On the tender mercies, Chrysostom explains the phrase as meaning according to Christ, so that Paul loves them not with natural bowels but with warmer ones, having become a father to them through the relationship in Christ. Ellicott calls the expression striking and even startling, an emanation faint but true from the heart of Jesus Christ dwelling in him; Wesley reaches the same point in a sentence, that in Paul not Paul lives but Jesus Christ, so that he longs with the tenderness not of Paul but of Christ. Calvin sets the phrase against carnal affection, which has respect to its own advantage and changes with the seasons, and cites a note deriving the term from a Hebrew word for all tender and as it were motherly affections. Barnes explains only the physiology, the heart and lungs being regarded as the seat of compassion.
9:
Two reach for the same figure and pull it opposite ways. Clarke wants the love to be a river fed with rain and fresh streams, swelling until it fills its banks and floods the adjacent plains; Robertson keeps the flood but adds the banks, a perpetual overflowing with necessary limitations. Wesley marks the same restlessness: the fire which burned in the apostle never says, it is enough. Barnes observes what is not asked for: not riches or worldly prosperity but spiritual blessings only, and he wants their love intelligent rather than blind, in proportion to the relative value of things. Henry adds that those who abound much in any grace still need to abound more. Ellicott presses the verb, which means to overflow: love shall not merely fill the heart but overflow from the emotional into the intellectual part, becoming, as it does in simple and loving characters, a means of spiritual insight. Calvin pauses to dismiss a reading in which your love would be a title of address for the Philippians, as illiterate persons say your reverence: no such expression occurs in Paul, nor had such fooleries then come into use. Clarke and Wesley take the second word for spiritual feeling, Wesley adding that we must be inwardly sensible of divine peace and joy or we cannot know what they are.

On the next clause Barnes says the margin gives the sense better, to try the things that differ rather than approve things that are excellent, and Gill runs out the pairs, morality and grace, law and gospel, the doctrines of men and of Christ. Ellicott keeps the received rendering: the word carries the idea of distinctive excellence, conspicuous amid what is evil or defective, and to test is first to distinguish the best and then prove its absolute goodness. Henry gives both. On sincerity Barnes offers two derivations, what is judged of in sunshine, and, for the English word, without wax, honey pure and transparent; Ellicott makes it purity tested and found clear of base admixtures, the sincerity not of unconscious innocence but of well-tried purity, proof even against suspicion. The following word is ambiguous, and Ellicott and Calvin part. Ellicott prefers the sense of giving no offence, at which none will stumble; Calvin reports that exposition from an ancient authority without rejecting it, but prefers the passive sense, that they may go forward in their calling with unwavering step, since we all know from experience how many stumbling blocks Satan throws in the way.

The fruits of righteousness raise a question of grammar and one of doctrine. Ellicott notes that the participle is properly having been filled, so that it refers not to the future day of Christ but to the whole time that day will complete, and on that ground makes the fruit righteousness itself rather than its product. Calvin guards the other side, that it does not follow there is righteousness wherever there are its fruits, since there is none before God without complete obedience to the law, found in no saint; what is wanting is supplied through the remission of sins, so that all righteousness still depends on faith. He adds the grafting image, that we are wild and unproductive until ingrafted into Christ, whose living root makes us fruitbearing trees. Wesley finds three properties in the verse: sincerity must bear fruit, must bear so abundantly as to fill us, and branch and fruit alike derive their being from the root. Barnes denies that liberality alone is meant and names the fruits as honesty, truth, kindness, meekness and goodness, adding that the service of the lips is easy and a life of patient piety far harder. Gill explains why they are called fruits, as springing from an incorruptible seed and owing everything to the dews of grace; Clarke reads the participle as filled up and filled full, the whole soul and life occupied.
12:
The difficulty answered here is the offence of the cross. Henry states it as the Philippians might have felt it: if this doctrine were of God, he would not suffer one so active in preaching it to be thrown by as a despised broken vessel; the answer is that the word of God is not bound, and that here is a strange chemistry of Providence, extracting the enlargement of the gospel out of the confinement of the apostle. Calvin makes it a standing fault in us: we allow Christ crucified to be preached, but when he appears with his cross we are thunderstruck at the novelty and either avoid him or hold him in abhorrence, and that in the persons of those who bring us the gospel as well as our own. Barnes explains why the report was sent: they were attached to him, rumours might reach them, and he had good news. Ellicott lists what had happened since they parted, the arrest at Jerusalem and the captivity at Caesarea and then at Rome, and suggests that his acquaintance with the soldiers there prepared an opening he could not otherwise have found.

What the praetorium means divides them. Barnes argues for the emperor's palace, because provincials used the word for the chief magistrate's residence and because the greetings from Caesar's household later in the letter suggest the gospel had reached the imperial family; others, he notes, prefer the praetorian camp. Clarke and Calvin take it of the palace, Calvin naming Nero's and supporting himself with an excursus deriving the word from the general's tent. Ellicott sets out the choices, the palace, the barrack attached to it, or the camp outside, notes that the ancient commentators take the first but that it agrees badly with the statement in Acts that Paul dwelt in his own hired house, and concludes with a modern scholar for a body of men rather than a place, the praetorian guard; the following words, he adds, mean not in all other places but to all the rest. Robertson agrees, describing the ten thousand picked soldiers whose favour emperors had to court, and reports that others argue for the imperial court's judicial authorities. Barnes dwells on the chain: who would wish to be bound night and day to a living witness of all he did, a spy on all his movements, never at liberty to be alone. Gill observes the bonds were not for debt, nor for any capital crime.

Why the brethren grew bolder is variously answered. Barnes offers four possibilities: that they were roused by the imprisonment of so distinguished a champion, that popular feeling had turned towards Christianity, that they had met him in his hired house, or that some seized a chance to set themselves up as preachers who would have been restrained had he been at liberty; and he adds an old commentator's suggestion that seeing him bear such things with pleasure they concluded the gospel must be divine. Henry takes the generous line, that they could gladly suffer in Paul's company, that what the enemy meant to discourage the preachers was overruled for their encouragement, and that seeing the worst of it they were not afraid to venture. Calvin generalises it, that the tortures of the saints are a ground of confidence to us: a spectacle of nothing but the rage of persecutors would dishearten, but seeing the hand of the Lord make his people unconquerable under the cross we have a pledge of our own victory. Ellicott divides the effect between the two sorts of preachers described next, the one trusting in the captivity for the scope it gave, the other finding in it evil overruled to good; and he and Robertson both attach the words in the Lord to the confidence rather than the brethren. Wesley and Clarke make the constancy the cause.
15:
Who these rivals were is agreed by most, denied by one. Barnes thinks them Judaizing teachers, professing Christianity, who held that Paul's views derogated from the honour of Moses and the law, and who took the chance of his confinement, since he could not confute them before the people. Clarke says the same and adds that they probably denounced him to the Jews at Rome as an enemy to the law; he also restricts the word preach, which here means only that they proclaimed Jesus as the Messiah, not that they were preachers of the gospel in our sense. Ellicott finds the same identification impossible to doubt, pointing to the Judaic element in Roman Christianity and to the apostle's doubt of his reception as he approached the city, so that the party of Cephas and the party of Paul might stand in sharper antagonism there than at Corinth. Robertson calls it petty personal jealousy, and adds that jealousy is always against those of one's own class or profession, as preachers with preachers and doctors with doctors. Gill dissents: these were brethren and members of the church, whom the apostle owns as brethren in the ministry and in whose preaching he rejoices, which could not be if they were unbelievers.

On not sincerely, Ellicott says the version misleads, since the original is not purely, and the apostle imputes to them not hypocrisy but an admixture of partisanship. Calvin argues the same from the context, that the term does not apply to doctrine, since a man who teaches most purely may not be of a sincere mind, and Paul would have felt no pleasure in seeing the gospel corrupted. He then raises two questions. How could such preaching injure the apostle? Many occasions are unknown to us, being unacquainted with the circumstances of the time. And why should men persecute a doctrine they approve? Because ambition is blind, nay, a furious beast; and he adds that he has seen the like, men preaching the gospel only to gratify the rage of the wicked against pious pastors. On adding affliction Barnes says how they did it is unknown, though the ancient expositors thought they preached so as to excite the multitude against him; Ellicott adopts it, notes the true text says to stir up rather than add, and suggests they worked on his jailors. Clarke observes that many manuscripts transpose the two verses.

The rejoicing that follows is what everyone dwells on. Ellicott draws the governing distinction: the apostle speaks of the motives of the preachers, not the substance of their preaching, and for the latter he cares much and for the former nothing, whereas where rejection of his authority was bound up with rejection of his doctrine he rebukes it vehemently. Barnes turns it into a rule for ministers: a man laid aside by sickness should rejoice that others are in health, one who is unpopular should rejoice in another's success, and even when others preach what we count error we may rejoice, since in the error we cannot but in the naming of a Saviour we can; the most stammering announcement that man has a Saviour may save a soul, where ignorance could save none. Calvin agrees that God sometimes does an admirable work by depraved instruments, and instances a man of his own day whom he calls a profligate villain and yet thanks God for using; but he sets a limit, that had the matter been in Paul's hand he would never have ordained such persons, nor are they to be accounted Christ's lawful ministers. Chrysostom begins higher up: nothing in this life can fix its fangs on a lofty soul, which flies as to a mighty fortress; such was Paul's, who had the emperor for an enemy and yet says he will rejoice not for a season but always. Gill and Wesley keep to the two motives.
19:
What the salvation is divides them, and one names his opponents. Clarke takes it of temporal safety: when the gospel came to be understood the Romans would see that a man who proclaimed a prince whose kingdom was not of this world, and who taught that tribute should be paid, could be no enemy to Caesar. Barnes rejects that view and names Clarke among those who hold it, since Paul was not certain of release and could not have expected it from the supply of the Spirit; he takes the trials themselves as among the means of his salvation. Ellicott takes the word as safety rather than salvation from sin, shown either in life by his release or in death by his coming home to Christ, so that either way he is safe from all enmity. Calvin says flatly that what follows shows he means no bodily safety, and Wesley reads a higher degree of glory. Robertson takes it of release, reports that a modern scholar takes it of eternal salvation because the next verse suits that better, and asks whether Paul carried both conceptions in the word.

Calvin adds a caution about the two things joined here. Because prayer and the supply of the Spirit stand in one connection we must not suppose them alike: the supply is the efficient cause and prayer a subordinate help, and nothing is detracted from the unmerited goodness of God on which our prayers themselves depend. He notes that the word rendered supply means the furnishing of what is wanting, and that the Spirit is called the Spirit of Christ because he was poured on him in all fullness that he might give out to each member by measure; Clarke takes the word as furnishing whatever was needed for the trials before the judgment seat. On the earnest expectation Barnes insists the desire was not primarily for release but that in all circumstances he might honour the gospel, life being the secondary consideration. Ellicott catches a fine turn: when the apostle speaks of the chance of failure he uses the first person, I shall be ashamed, but when of triumph it is Christ who shall be magnified, since failure could only be his own fault and triumph his Master's strength. He notes too that the word body rather than flesh is chosen because in the New Testament the body is always that in which we may glorify God.

The famous saying is read four ways. Barnes takes it of a single purpose, to know Christ, to imitate him, to make him known and to enjoy him, pursued with as much singleness as a miser pursues gold; no believer, he adds, will regret at death having lived so, though many regret that they did not. Ellicott makes it a matter of state rather than principle, the whole concrete condition of life being so lived in Christ that it becomes a manifestation of his presence, which is the result where the other passages give the cause. Robertson keeps to the grammar, that living is coextensive with Christ, and that to die is to cash in both principal and interest and so have more of Christ than when living. Calvin dissents from all of them, saying interpreters have hitherto given a wrong rendering, since he makes Christ the subject of both clauses, so that Christ is gain in life and in death alike, a word being left to be understood as the Greeks allow; the sense is fuller so, for Christ alone makes us happy in death and in life, and without him a miserable death is matched by a life no happier. Clarke reads it the same way, that whether he live or die Christ is gain, and Henry reports that reading alongside the usual one. Gill makes Christ the author, object and end of his life, preferring the last as the sense here.
22:
The sentence about living in the flesh is broken, and they say so. Ellicott calls the Authorised rendering inaccurate and perhaps a gloss meant to soften the difficulty, and says the construction is broken by emotion or absorption in thought and can only be supplied by conjecture; the sense is plain, that to live still in the flesh carries a fruit of apostolical labour in souls brought to Christ, a harvest whose gain outweighs his own. Robertson notes that there is no word for if in the Greek, and that the verb rendered I wot not usually means to make known, so that it makes good sense to read, I do not declare what I shall choose. Barnes reports the older renderings, that if his life were of use to the gospel it was worth an effort, but doubts they can be got out of the Greek; his own reading is that living would cost him labour, so that he could not tell whether to prefer an immediate departure or a longer life of toil. Wesley takes the plainer sense with delight, that the fruit of living longer is that he can labour more: glorious labour, desirable fruit.

On being in a strait Barnes takes the words from a ship at anchor when violent winds blow that would drive it to sea, his affection for them holding like the moorings while a heavenly influence bore upon him like the gale. Ellicott traces the word to the sense of being hemmed in, usually with an idea of distress and often of disease, and notes that our Lord uses it of mental distress in himself. Gill hears an allusion to David, put to choose among three judgments and saying he was in a great strait. Chrysostom is astonished at the hesitation. He confesses first that we all shudder at death, some by reason of many sins, of whom he says he is one, others from mere love of life; then he presses the apostle with questions. What trader whose vessel is full of untold wealth, when he may run into port and be at rest, would prefer to be still at sea? What general, who might be quit of war with trophies and refresh himself in the palace, would choose still to stand in battle array? Having rehearsed the shipwrecks and stripes and perils, he asks how a man whose life was so exceeding bitter could wish to remain in it.

Whether the confidence of the next verses was fulfilled is the sharpest question here. Clarke says plainly that after two years in bonds at Rome the apostle was released. Wesley goes further, calling the knowledge a prophetic notice given while he was writing, and says doubtless he did see them afterwards. Gill will not have it: the words are not certain knowledge from revelation but conjecture arising from the present state of things, and though some have thought he was set at liberty and travelled through several countries there is no sufficient proof. Barnes agrees the ground was neither a revelation nor intelligence from the palace but his belief that his life was needful to them, and warns that know is not to be pressed, since the letter elsewhere admits a doubt. Ellicott presses hardest, noting that the same word is used in Acts of a conviction which, so far as the history can be followed, was not verified, and concluding that apostolic inspiration, like the apostolic power of miracle, was a gift relative to the apostolic work and did not necessarily extend beyond it. Calvin answers those who think it inconsistent that so holy an apostle should be disappointed: their fears are groundless, for the saints regulate their expectations by the word of God and promise themselves no more than he has promised, holding a sure persuasion only where they have a sure token and expecting all else conditionally.
27:
The word rendered conversation is a civic one, and all say so. Ellicott renders it, use your citizenship worthily of the gospel, and finds the choice natural to a man contemplating the imperial city and writing to a Roman colony proud of its citizenship. Clarke reads the church at Philippi as a free or imperial city possessing great honours, and notes that the same figure returns later with heaven put in the place of the church, since no one outside the one has a right to the other. Barnes warns that the English word has narrowed to mean talking, whereas in Scripture it means conduct in general; the Greek is to live as a citizen, so the rule covers our duties in maintaining the laws and choosing rulers as well as our dress and business, and nothing we do or say is excepted. Henry and Clarke both take care over the striving: it is together and not one with another, a wrestling against the common adversary; and Henry adds that there may be oneness of heart where there is diversity of judgment, and that a man may sleep and go to hell, but he who will go to heaven must look about him and be diligent.

What the token is, and what it is a token of, is less settled. Ellicott refers it to their fearlessness, a real sign of divine strength made perfect in weakness, though not infallible, since it has often accompanied fanatic delusion; its effect on the heathen appears in the affected contempt with which the Stoics called it a kind of madness, a morbid habit, a sheer obstinacy. Clarke reports critics who refer the word to the faith of the gospel, which the heathen took for a token of perdition to all who embraced it. Barnes refers it to the persecution together with the constancy he hoped they would show, reading it as proof that the persecutors could not prevail and that the persecuted were Christ's friends. Calvin insists on the exact force of the word, a proof and not a cause, since Scripture nowhere teaches that the afflictions the saints endure cause their salvation. Robertson quotes another that the Christian gladiator does not anxiously await the signal of life or death from the fickle crowd.

That suffering is called a gift is where they linger. Calvin argues from it: the endurance of the cross is itself God's gift, and since all God's gifts are salutary the sufferings become evidences of his grace; persecutions are in a manner seals of adoption, and it is the highest honour divine grace confers that we should suffer reproach or death for his name, for in that case he arrays us in his livery. He does not pretend the lesson is learnt, adding that more will bid God retire with gifts of that nature than embrace the cross, and breaking off with a curse on our stupidity. Barnes takes the other half of the verse and enumerates why believing is itself a privilege: it is an honour to trust one who ought to be trusted, by it our sins are forgiven, and it saves the mind from the restlessness and gloom of a sceptic. Henry makes both gifts equal and says the disposition to believe is from God, yet guards the point in the same breath, that salvation must not be ascribed to bodily afflictions as though they deserved it, faith and patience being alike his gifts. He closes with the rule for martyrdom: it is not simply the suffering, but the cause, and not only the cause but the spirit, which makes the martyr, for a man may suffer in a good cause with a wrong mind and lose the value of it. Gill and Wesley keep to the encouragement, that neither the rage nor the cunning of adversaries should move them.
